primary_claim: A human-relative time-horizon metric, defined as the longest task duration over which an LLM exceeds METR's actual human-baseline reliability, is doubling every 1.9 months, much faster than METR's fixed 50%-reliability time-horizon trend's 6.8-7 month doubling time, implying human-level long-horizon software agency by roughly 2026-2027.
contradicts_or_qualifies: Qualifies AI-2027's claim that METR's fixed-reliability (80%) time-horizon trend is super-exponential with a finite-time blowup: finds this poorly supported for METR's own fixed-reliability metric, but much better supported once the metric is redefined relative to human baseline reliability.
stated_future_work: Collect higher-quality, better-incentivized human baseline measurements for long agentic tasks
Collect direct human measurements for much longer tasks than METR's current sub-1-day benchmark tasks
Redo the statistical (AIC) model-selection tests including the new Claude Opus 4.5 data point
limitations_stated: METR's human reliability baselines are widely regarded as weak or poorly incentivized, which undermines the human-relative metric that depends on them
AIC model-selection results for exponential vs hyperbolic fits are quite sensitive to which data points/outliers are included and should be taken with caution
Extrapolating the hyperbolic projection to human-level requires extrapolating the human logistic curve far beyond the durations actually tested in the METR benchmark
The very large (444-billion-minute) Claude Opus 4.5 horizon estimate is highly sensitive to estimation error since both LLM and human reliabilities are near zero at such long durations
The LLM logistic slope-parameter trend used in one alternative extrapolation is noisy (R^2 ~ 0.3)
quote: the LLM time horizons at human-reliability are doubling every 1.9 months, versus every 7 months over the same time period for the METR (50%-reliability) time horizon trend
